conventions.convention: Simple surfaces are compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian surfaces with smooth strictly convex boundary, no conjugate points, and finite forward and backward exit times for every interior unit geodesic.
Strict convexity uses the outward normal and g(∇w νout,w)>0. Incoming boundary vectors have strictly positive inner product with the inward normal; tangential vectors are excluded.
R(A,B)C=∇A∇BC−∇B∇AC−∇[A,B]C, and Jacobi fields satisfy Dt²J+R(J,γ̇)γ̇=0.
V generates positive fibre rotation, X⊥=[X,V], K=g(R(e1,e2)e2,e1), and the Liouville density is dVg dSx with incoming flux weight μ=g(v,νin).
The injectivity theorem concerns real smooth functions compactly supported in the interior; it requires no orientability assumption and asserts no stability estimate.
The sphere example uses integration over full closed great circles, distinct from the boundary-to-boundary transform.

load_bearing.statement: On an oriented simple surface, the geodesic flow preserves Liouville measure, the stated commutator and integration-by-parts identities and Santaló formula hold, the endpoint-zero normal index form is positive definite, and zero data for f∈Cc∞(M°) gives a smooth compactly supported transport primitive with Xu_f=−f.
For every real-valued u∈C∞(SM) with u=0 on ∂SM, ‖VXu‖²=‖XVu‖²−(KVu,Vu)+‖Xu‖² on an oriented simple surface.

Every connected component C of the tangent orientation double cover of a simple surface, with pullback metric, is compact, connected, oriented and simple, projects locally isometrically onto M, and satisfies I0,C(f∘π)(z̃)=I0,Mf(π(z̃)) for f∈Cc∞(M°).
For a real-valued f∈Cc∞(M°,ℝ) on a simple surface, I0f=0 on ∂+SM implies f=0 on M. No orientability assumption on M is required.
The tangent orientation double cover consists of pairs (x,ox), where ox is an orientation ray in det TxM, with the specified two-sheeted smooth boundary-chart structure and canonical orientation.

published_dependencies.used_for: Smooth positive-definite metrics, including boundaries where stated.
Metric compatibility and torsion freeness in flow, curvature, and variation calculations.
Unique Levi-Civita connection, including at a smooth boundary.
Jacobi equation and curvature sign convention.
Local geodesic ODE existence, uniqueness, and smooth dependence in extended charts.
Orientations as positive rays in determinant lines.
Local sheets of the orientation cover.
Smooth half-space charts and transitions.
Smooth tangent bundle and invertible tangent transitions at boundary points.
Coordinate expression and positivity of the base volume density.
Bracket-corrected curvature commutator.
Curvature argument order and positive round-sphere convention.
Unit-speed elapsed time equals curve length.
Distance as the infimum of curve lengths.
Positive separation of compact disjoint sets and triangle inequalities.
Compactness and neighborhood arguments using Riemannian distance, including boundaries.
Short geodesic segments near the boundary cannot reach the support of f.
Smooth dependence of transverse first exit times.
Compactness of the orientation double cover.
Surjectivity of each orientation-cover component and lifting geodesics through their exit times.
Paths joining base points in the connected surface.
Derivation of the Jacobi equation for the sphere variation.

concerns.concern: Proof 4.1 says “Every s-curve is geodesic, so D_t∂_tγ_s=0”. The geodesics are the t-curves with s fixed. The displayed equation and subsequent Jacobi calculation use the correct parameter; “s-curve” is a wording error.

seams_checked.note: The prerequisite distinguishes exact identifiability from quantitative stability. The assigned theorem proves only injectivity and makes no stability or estimator claim; there is no stronger item-level citation across this page edge.

The Euclidean disk example agrees with the Radon line-integral convention after identifying chord direction with the perpendicular line normal. No Euclidean Fourier inversion formula is asserted for general curved surfaces.
This is a page-level prerequisite. Scanning its item inventory found no direct citation of the assigned items, hence no strengthened restatement of their injectivity or geometric conclusions.

The simple-background definition agrees in dimension two. The coefficient-uniqueness corollary applies injectivity to q1−q2 with both potentials explicitly real and compactly supported in the interior; its observation-time hypothesis supplies all maximal-ray data.

The transversal example preserves the real compact-support injectivity domain. The four-factor lemma's F1 loosely describes simplicity through unique segments, but F5 explicitly supplies the equivalence and unique-geodesic consequences as a separate external input; these are not inferred solely from the assigned definition.
